wrap.e: From Middle English wrappen (“to wrap, fold”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to North Frisian wrappe (“to press into.
wrap.g: To enclose (an object) completely in any flexible, thin material such as fabric or paper.

wrap.e: From Middle English wrappe, from the verb (see above).
wrap.g: Paper or sheeting that is wrapped around something to protect, contain, or conceal it.

wrapped.e: From Spotify Wrapped, launched in 2016, which popularised the concept.
wrapped.g: A feature on a website or online service that includes a summary of a user's activity on the service during a given year, created by logging

wrath.e: Effectively analysable as wroth + -th (abstract nominal suffix); compare Dutch wreedte.
wrath.g: Great anger; (countable) an instance of this.

wrath.e: A variant of wroth, probably influenced by wrath (noun) (see etymology 1).
wrath.g: Synonym of wroth (“full of anger; wrathful”).

wrathful.e: From Middle English wrattheful, wrathful; by surface analysis, wrath + ful.
wrathful.g: Possessed of great wrath; very angry.

wreak.e: From Middle English wreken, from Old English wrecan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“push, shove, drive, track down”).
wreak.g: To cause harm; to afflict; to inflict; to harm or injure; to let out harm.

wreak.e: From Middle English wreke, wrake, Northern Middle English variants of wreche, influenced later by Etymology 1, above.

wreath.e: From Middle English wreth, wrethe (“coiled or rounded shape; decorative garland, wreath; chaplet, crown; ring”, noun), from Old English *wreoþa, wriþa (“band, coil, ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *wriþō, from Proto-Germanic *wriþô, from *wrīþaną (“to twist; to weave”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyt- (“to twist”).

wreck.e: From Middle English wrek, from Anglo-Norman wrek, from Old Norse *wrek (whence Norwegian rek, Icelandic rek, Swedish vrak, Danish vrag), from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną (“to pursue”, whence Old English wrecan (English wreak), Old Saxon wrekan, Old High German rëhhan, Gothic 𐍅𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (wrikan)), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to track; to hunt; to follow”).
wreck.g: Something or someone that has been ruined.

wrench.e: From Middle English wrench, from Old English wrenċ, from Proto-Germanic *wrankiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wreng- (“to turn”).
wrench.g: A movement that twists or pulls violently; a tug.

wrench.e: From Middle English wrenchen, from Old English wrenċan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrankijan, from Proto-Germanic *wrankijaną.

wrest.e: From Middle English wresten, wrasten, wræsten, from Old English wrǣstan (“to twist forcibly, wrench”), from Proto-Germanic *wraistijaną, (compare Proto-Germanic *wrīhaną (“to turn, wind; to cover, envelop”), *wrīþaną (“to weave, twist”), Old Norse reista (“to bend, twist”)).

Possibly a variant of wrist: see the quotation. Wrist is also derived from *wrīþaną (“to weave, twist”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *wreiḱ-, *wreyḱ- (“to bend, twist”), *wreyt- (“to bend”).
wrest.g: A partition in a water wheel by which the form of the buckets is determined.

wrestle.e: By surface analysis, wrest + -le (frequentative suffix). Probably related to wraxle (UK, dialectal, archaic).
wrestle.g: To take part in (a wrestling bout or match).

wrestling.g: A sport where two opponents attempt to subdue each other in bare-handed grappling using techniques of leverage, holding, and pressure points

wretch.e: From Middle English wrecche, from Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, fugitive, warrior”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to track, follow”).
wretch.g: An unhappy, unfortunate, or miserable person.

wretched.e: From Middle English wrecched (“(adjective) characterized by or suffering hardship or misfortune, miserable, unfortunate, unhappy; indigent, poor; of low economic or social status, lowly; (noun) miserable person”), from wrecche (“characterized by or suffering hardship or misfortune, miserable, unfortunate, unhappy; indigent, poor.
wretched.g: Characterized by or feeling deep affliction or distress; very miserable.

wretchedness.e: From Middle English wrecchednesse; equivalent to wretched + -ness.
wretchedness.g: An unhappy state of mental or physical suffering.

wring.e: From Middle English wring, wringe, wringen, wryng, wrynge, wryngen, wryngyn, from Old English wringan (“to wring”), from Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, twist, wring”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrenǵʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”).
wring.g: Often followed by out: to squeeze or twist (something moist) tightly so that liquid is forced out.

wring.e: Partly: from Middle English wring, wringe (“twisting or wringing (of the neck)”), from Middle English wringen, wryngen (verb); and from the modern English verb.
wring.g: A powerful squeezing or twisting action.

wringing.e: From Middle English wryngynge; equivalent to wring + -ing.
wringing.g: The act by which something is wrung.

wrinkle.e: From Middle English wrinkle, wrynkel (“crease, fold, wrinkle”), from the verb (see below).
wrinkle.g: A small furrow, ridge or crease in an otherwise smooth surface.

wrinkle.e: From Middle English wrynklen, wrinklen (“to wrinkle”), from Old English *wrinclian (attested in past participle ġewrinclod (“wrinkled, crooked, winding”)).
wrinkle.g: To make wrinkles in; to cause to have wrinkles.

wrist.e: From Middle English wrist, from Old English wrist, from Proto-West Germanic *wristu, from Proto-Germanic *wristuz (compare Old Frisian wrist, Low German Wrist, German Rist (“back of hand, instep, withers”), Swedish vrist), from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną (“to twist, turn”).
wrist.g: The complex joint between forearm bones, carpus, and metacarpals where the hand is attached to the arm; the carpus in a narrow sense.

write.e: From Middle English writen, from Old English wrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrītan, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną (“to carve, write”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey- (“to rip, tear”).
write.g: To form letters, words or symbols on a surface in order to communicate.

writer.e: From Middle English writer, writere, from Old English wrītere (“draughtsman; painter; writer; scribe; copyist”) and ġewritere (“writer; composer”), equivalent to write + -er.
writer.g: A person who writes, or produces literary work; an author can refer to themselves as "the writer".

writhe.e: From Middle English writhen, from Old English wrīþan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrīþan, from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną (“to weave, twist, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyt- (“to twist, writhe”).

writing.e: From Middle English writinge, wrytynge, writende, writand, from Old English wrītende, present participle of Old English wrītan (“to scratch, carve, write”), equivalent to write + -ing.

written.g: Of, relating, or characteristic of writing (i.e., of that which has been written).

wrong.e: From Middle English wrong, from Old English wrang (“wrong, twisted, uneven”), from Old Norse rangr, vrangr (“crooked, wrong”), from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz (“crooked, twisted, turned awry”), from Proto-Indo-European *werḱ-, *wrengʰ- (“to twist, weave, tie together”), from *wer- (“to turn, bend”).

wrongdoer.g: Someone who does wrong, whether morally, ethically, or in contravention of a law.

wrongdoing.e: From Middle English wrong doyng, wrong doynge, wrong doinge, equivalent to wrong + doing.

wrongfully.e: From Middle English wrongfully, wrongfullich; equivalent to wrongful + -ly.

wroth.e: From Middle English wroth, wrooth, from Old English wrāþ, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþaz (“cruel”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyt- (“to turn”).

wrought.e: The past participle of Middle English worchen (“to work”), from Old English wyrċan (past tense worhte, past participle (ġe)worht; cf. also the metathetic variant (ġe)wroht), from Proto-West Germanic *wurkijan, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to work”).
wrought.g: Having been worked or prepared somehow.

work.e: From Middle English work, werk, from Old English weorc, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to make”).

From Middle English werken and worchen, from Old English wyrċan and wircan (Mercian), from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥ǵyéti (“to be working, to be at work”), from the root *werǵ-.
work.g: To do a specific task by employing physical or mental powers.
